beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection URI from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI), never hardcode it, never print it to logs, and load it at process start so the app can create a single shared MongoClient/connection pool that is reused by all requests.

Create a singleton MongoClient with explicit connection pool sizing (e.g., maxPoolSize=50) and sensible timeouts (connectTimeoutMS, serverSelectionTimeoutMS) rather than constructing a new client per request; reuse that client in Flask/worker threads.

Do not store DocumentDB credentials in source code or repo; use environment variables and prefer a secrets manager (Azure Key Vault) for production, fetching secrets at startup rather than embedding them in files.
Use SCRAM-SHA-256 or the strongest supported MongoDB authentication mechanism available for the cluster; ensure TLS/SSL is enabled for the connection string and reject insecure connections.

Store embeddings in a dedicated field (e.g., embedding: [float,...]) with a fixed dimensionality per collection, and store metadata (ticket id, kb_id, text, created_at, customer_id, pass/fail tags) as separate indexed fields to support efficient filtering and retrieval.
Keep vector dimensionality consistent; validate embedding length at write time and reject or pad/trim inconsistent vectors so the vector index remains consistent.
When using cosine similarity with HNSW, store L2-normalized vectors (unit length) so retrieval can use dot-product equivalently and results are stable across embedding sources.

Create a server-side vector index (HNSW or DiskANN) on the embedding field with tuned parameters: choose M (e.g., 8–48) and efConstruction (e.g., 100–500) during index build to balance build time and recall, and set ef (search ef) at query time (e.g., 16–128) to trade speed vs recall.
When creating the vector index, build it in the background or during a maintenance window and avoid blocking normal traffic; for large corpora use incremental or batched indexing if supported.

Use server-side vector search operator / index-enabled query to return only top-k ids and scores and project only needed metadata (text, kb_id) instead of returning full documents, to reduce network transfer and costs.

Add secondary indexes on common filter fields used together with vector search (e.g., customer_id, product, language, created_at) so you can restrict the ANN search to a smaller candidate set; create compound indexes when you filter+sort by fields.

Use bulk/batched writes (bulk_write) when seeding or updating many documents (embeddings) to minimize round trips and to avoid exceeding connection/memory limits; chunk large loads into batches of a few hundred to a few thousand depending on payload size.

Implement exponential backoff and retry logic for transient network and rate-limit errors (e.g., MongoNetworkError, timeout, 429) with jitter, and make index/insert operations idempotent or track progress to safely retry bulk operations.
Avoid returning embeddings to the client; only return IDs, scores and short metadata. If embeddings must be exported for offline use, do it via a controlled bulk export process with RBAC/auditing.

Use deterministic pseudo-embeddings only for local unit tests and CI; in any integration or production scenario use a real embedding model and store a model identifier and version with each vector so you can reindex if the model changes.

Limit per-request result sizes and apply server-side limits/skip rather than retrieving full collections; for RAG retrieve top-N (e.g., 5) summaries only and assemble prompt server-side, truncating to a configured token/context budget.

Record provenance and scoring metadata with each suggested resolution (source_doc_ids, retrieval_scores, model_version, timestamp) to support auditability and feedback loops; persist suggestions and outcomes for later re-training or tuning.

Provision cluster capacity and storage to account for vector indexes (index memory and disk are significant); when using HNSW increase instance/compute tier or RU provisioning for indexing and high-QPS searches to avoid throttling.

Use projection to exclude large text fields or binary blobs from queries where not needed, and store large textual content in a separate field or collection if you only need summaries for retrieval to reduce I/O and network costs.
Create a TTL index (expireAfterSeconds) for ephemeral collections (like temporary ticket sessions) to automatically purge stale documents and control storage growth.

Instrument and monitor query performance and index usage (slow queries, query plan analysis) using the provider’s tools (MCP/cluster diagnostics and Azure Monitor) and adjust index parameters or provisioning based on observed latency and RU consumption.

When creating/updating indexes and embeddings, perform these operations under a maintenance flag or write-quiesce mode in the app to avoid serving inconsistent retrieval results to users until reindex completes.

When doing retrieval-augmented generation, sanitize and truncate retrieved context, include only the most relevant passages, and use prompt engineering with explicit instructions and token budgets to avoid hallucinations and stay within LLM input limits.
Use RBAC and least-privilege credentials for client apps: give the service account only the collections and ops it needs (read for inference, write for seeding), and rotate credentials regularly.
